narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 60.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. First, your family's upper-middle income bracket pushed the prediction toward failure. Although this is the most common income group among accepted students (45%), the model associated it with a noticeably higher risk of not passing the bar. Second, your strong performance in your third year of law school worked in your favor and pulled the prediction toward passing; you ranked in the top decile, well above the average of accepted students. Third, your LSAT score of 45 also increased the chance of failure. While this score is higher than the average of 37 among accepted students, the model still interpreted it as contributing to a greater likelihood of struggling on the bar.

Taken together, the negative influence from your family income and LSAT outweighed the positive signal from your excellent third-year grades, resulting in the rejection.

You should consider retaking the LSAT to aim for an even higher score, or strengthening other parts of your profile that signal bar exam readiness. Many students improve their outcomes on a second application cycle after targeted preparation.
